summary: An IAB statement of concern about voice traffic that does not slow down when the network is congested. It raises worries about fairness to other traffic, the quality users experience, and the danger of congestion collapse. It makes no recommendations about how to deploy voice over IP.

eli5.summary: If everyone talking on a road never slows down when it gets crowded, traffic jams for all. The authors worry phone calls on the internet might do that.

questions: why does voip need congestion control
when should a voip call stop sending
what are iab concerns about voice traffic
subtitle: The IAB warns that voice traffic which never slows down on a congested link can hurt everyone, and says when it should stop.

tldr.problem: Voice over IP is sometimes sent as best-effort traffic over congested links, and voice flows with a fixed minimum sending rate cannot slow down further when many packets are being dropped. The IAB worries about congestion collapse, poor call quality and unfairness to TCP.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC compares a voice flow at its minimum rate with a TCP connection sending at the same rate on the wire, and uses the packet drop rate that TCP could survive to decide when the voice flow should terminate or suspend.
tldr.outcome: It recommends that IETF standards for best-effort flows with a minimum sending rate specify a drop rate above which the flow stops or suspends. It is not a complete protocol specification.

today: RFC 3714 is an Informational RFC, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an IAB statement of concern and a recommendation to the IETF community, not a protocol specification.

sections.title: The IAB's Concern
sections.content:
This document gives IAB concerns about end-to-end congestion control for best-effort voice traffic. Voice service over best-effort broadband connections is already available, while end-to-end QoS is not generally available to customers. The RFC does not recommend deployment paths for VoIP in terms of QoS, does not claim that best-effort service gives acceptable VoIP performance, and does not discuss signalling.

The worry is that fast growth in real-time voice traffic that does not practise end-to-end congestion control could cause congestion collapse, unfairness and poor quality. The concerns also apply to video and other best-effort real-time traffic with a minimum sending rate, but the document focuses on audio. RFC 2914 already makes the point that best-effort traffic requires end-to-end congestion control.
sections.eli5: Many people already make phone calls over the ordinary Internet. If those calls never back off when the network is busy, the network could get into trouble.

sections.title: The Nairobi Example
sections.content:
At a November 2002 IEPREP meeting in Atlanta, a VoIP call was demonstrated between a hotel room in Atlanta and Nairobi, Kenya. Quality was very good, and the presentation said VoIP received good quality with packet drop rates of 5-40%. The call used a G.711 codec plus proprietary FEC and RTP/UDP/IP framing, so the traffic was substantially more than the 64 kbps the codec needs. The main congestion point was a 128 kbps access link shared by several subscribers, so the one call used more than half of it.

The RFC argues that a flow persisting at 64 kbps through a 40% drop rate serves neither its own users nor other users of the link. It also argues that universal overprovisioning is not an acceptable generic answer, because an overprovisioned core does not fix congested access links. There are two ways to avoid collapse: call rejection in busy periods, or end-to-end congestion control. Since best-effort traffic has no call acceptance mechanism, only congestion control is left.
sections.eli5: One call used more than half of a small shared pipe in Kenya. It sounded good, but the other people sharing the pipe had much less room.

sections.title: Why Persistent High Drop Rates Hurt
sections.content:
The RFC names three problems with persistent, high packet drop rates.

  • Congestion collapse. First seen in the mid 1980s, it happens when flows cross several congested links and packets that are dropped later have already wasted bandwidth earlier. It is a risk when both ends of a call are on congested broadband links, or the call crosses a congested backbone or transoceanic link.
  • User quality. With N flows of at least 64 kbps sharing a 128 kbps link, at least a fraction (N-2)/N of arriving traffic is dropped, and the drops are random, so everyone's quality suffers. One rule of thumb is that above 20% loss, audio quality is degraded beyond usefulness.
  • Fairness. A TCP flow sees the same drop rate but sends well under 64 kbps, so the voice traffic crowds it out.

The RFC assumes fairness against a TCP connection with the same round-trip time, 1460-byte packets and a minimum retransmit timeout of 100 ms. It rejects the claim that VoIP is inherently more important than other best-effort traffic, noting the network cannot judge the value of traffic. ISPs remain free to allocate bandwidth to traffic classes as they choose.
sections.eli5: When too many calls squeeze into a small pipe, most of the audio is lost for everyone, and web pages and email loaded with TCP get squeezed out too.

sections.title: What the IETF Was Already Doing
sections.content:
The RFC points to four efforts. The revised RTP profile, RFC 3551, says receivers SHOULD monitor loss and that loss is acceptable if a TCP flow in the same conditions would get at least the same throughput. The IAB comments that a MUST would be more appropriate for RTP traffic sharing links with other traffic, since congestion collapse is a danger to the Internet.

TFRC (RFC 3448) is equation-based congestion control with smoother throughput than TCP, but it is designed for fixed packet sizes. A variant for fixed rate and varying packet size, TFRC-PS, was still to be specified. DCCP offers CCID 2 (TCP-like) and CCID 3 (TFRC), and the RFC expects a CCID 4 for TFRC-PS. Adaptive codecs such as AMR, with eight modes between 4.75 and 12.2 kbps, can lower their rate under congestion, while codecs like G.711 were designed for circuit-switched networks. The RFC leaves Differentiated Services and signalling work aside.
sections.eli5: Other groups were already building ways for audio programs to slow down politely, and codecs that can use fewer bits when the road is crowded.

sections.title: When a Voice Flow Should Stop
sections.content:
A flow at its minimum sending rate cannot slow down further. The RFC proposes comparing it with TCP. With 40-byte headers (IP, RTP and UDP or DCCP), application data of N bytes per second in M packets per second gives B = N+40M bytes per second on the wire. Find the rate in packets per round-trip time of a TCP connection with the same B, and ask whether TCP could keep that rate at the observed drop rate D. If the voice flow sends much more than TCP could, it should terminate or suspend.

For a 4.75 kbps flow (N=593, M=20, B=1393) with a 0.1 second round-trip time, that is about 0.09 packets per round trip, and the flow should stop when the drop rate significantly exceeds 40%. For a 64 kbps flow (N=8000, M=50, B=10000) with the same round-trip time, the threshold is about 25%.

The RFC leaves open how long a rate is measured (for example at least five seconds), whether flows terminate or only suspend, and when to resume. A simple heuristic is to stop when the RTCP-reported loss exceeds 30% or N back-to-back reports are missing. It also notes that if routers mark packets with ECN instead of dropping them, only fairness remains a concern.
sections.eli5: A call that cannot get any quieter should hang up for a bit when the road is so jammed that even a patient web download could not keep going. Fast calls give up sooner than slow ones.

sections.title: Constraints and Recommendations
sections.content:
Voice cannot scale its packet rate much. Fewer packets means more audio per packet and harder error concealment, any error longer than a phoneme (typically 40 to 100 ms) is unrecoverable, and lower-rate codecs are generally more sensitive to loss.

The RFC makes two recommendations. First, IETF standards for best-effort flows with a minimum sending rate must specify a packet drop rate above which the flow terminates or suspends. Second, that rate should be consistent with the approach and tables in the document. Adaptive variable-bit-rate codecs are preferable, and ECN could help, though more mechanisms would be needed before UDP applications could safely use it. The RFC states that this is a recommendation to the IETF community and not a complete protocol specification. Its security section says the document creates no new security issues.
sections.eli5: The IAB asks that any rulebook for calls that cannot slow down must also say when the call should pause. It is advice for rule writers, not a finished rule.
